    What changed in v25

    What changed in v24: less to read, and a cleaner page. The round numbers are out of the text (the history stays here and in the appendix), long captions fold behind More, and the notes on how the media wall's layout was chosen moved to the appendix. The plan page has a new look: each section in its own card, a contents list down the side on a computer (a row of chips on a phone) that follows where you are, a floating tab bar, clearer tables, and a footer with the downloads. The plan itself doesn't change.
    v23: more ways to build the chairs in, and the room as it really is. Chairs built into the table (Dining wall chapter): as well as the chair cupboard, four chairs can hang behind the folded top on a deeper backboard, out of sight, and a fold-down oak seat can go in the gap at the stair end, a fifth place that's always there. Both are options for you to choose, and both are in the fit proof. Under the stairs is a brick side wall with plasterboard beneath, as you said: drawn in brick, so chairs five and six go in the garage. Your sofa's ottoman, square, blue corduroy, the size of one of its seats, is on the rug beside the coffee table (and moves in Edit room). Your sockets are drawn where they are: the single in the corner in front of the left Xbox game drawer (the one the plan makes a double), a double behind the sofa's short side, below and left of the PC, which now powers the rear speakers (the 12-way strip is off the buy list), and a double behind the plant stand in the window corner, for your lamp and the grow lights. The floating banister end at the top of the stairs is gone. The plan page has a new colour and four page looks (Card Room, Oak & linen, Sofa blue, Plain) and larger text to choose from; the questions are a list now, with no answer boxes; and the 3D room has six more suggestions to switch on or off (twelve in all).

    Built to your alcove: 186 wide, 38 deep, 235 to the ceiling

    • Base: 3 cm filler, three 60 cm bays, 3 cm filler. Bays 1 and 2 are IKEA BESTÅ 60×40×64 frames on a 9 cm plinth (tops at 73, back panels off); bay 3 is an 18 mm ply carcass 60 × 40 × 73 from the floor, split by a 12 mm divider into the slim game column (two face-out game drawers and the pads drawer) and the LP column (two face-out LP crates) under the turntable. One oak face frame runs across all three; its bottom rail hides the plinth and a hidden drawer under bay 2 with a finger pull (no push-to-open at floor level).
    • Depth: 40 cm frames, a 4 cm cable channel behind and the 2 cm face frame make 46 cm from the back wall, 8 cm proud of the chimney breast.
    • Worktop: solid oak, 186 × 46 × 3, top at 76, with a brush-lined slot behind the TV and a grommet behind the deck.
    • Oak uprights: 4.5 × 30 cm, 159 cm from the worktop to the ceiling. The left one stands against the side wall at 0–4.5, a corner post that frames the TV and carries the wrap ledge. The right one is at 131–135.5. That leaves 126.5 cm between them, 2.15 cm clear of the TV each side.
    • TV: centre 67.75 cm from the side wall (it was 93), on LG's stand set 2 cm off the back wall: bottom 81.4, centre 116.5, top 151.7. The soundbar sits centred under it at the worktop's front edge.
    • The turntable zone: 50.5 cm between the right upright and the breast. The deck sits on the worktop with 2.65 cm each side and its lid opens to about 121. Above it is an oak shelf at 134, through-tenoned into the upright, carrying the Series X on its fan stand; the phono preamp hangs underneath at the back.
    • Shelves above: the record ledge at 155.4 between the uprights, four LPs face-out; the high shelf at 196, wall to wall in two lengths, with books, a box, a print, a small framed sleeve and Deco B.
    • Bay 2 with the sub: the PS3 keeps the top row. Below its shelf the bay splits: on the left the sub's column, 23.4 cm wide, then a 12 mm ply divider, then 32.2 cm for the PS2 over the PS1 on a part shelf. The sub stands on a 3 cm isolation riser with 1 cm each side and 2.9 above. Its front is flush with the face frame, so its driver faces the room and its rear port has 15.6 cm to the wall.
    • Power: the side-wall socket in front of bay 1 becomes a double. Its two leads enter through a notch at the left end of the face frame's bottom rail and run back through the plinth to the channel.
    The media wall, looked over again

Sit the bar 2 cm proud of the stand's foot so the beam from the sofa clears it; LG's Magic Remote works by radio once paired, so it doesn't mind either way (a check in the fit proof).

    The sub in the media wall

    You asked for the sub back in the unit, with the Xbox bricks moved behind. It fits, and it sits in the best spot for it: under the TV, beside the soundbar, so the bass comes from the same place as the picture. Here's how the base makes room, and what was checked.

    • The bricks go to the back. The Xbox One's brick (17 × 7.5 × 4.811) and the Xbox 360's (allowed 21 × 10 × 616) lie flat at the back of their shelves, by the channel's power leads. Microsoft asks for a ventilated space, flat on the rubber pads, with nothing on top26; the bays are open front and back.
    • That frees bay 1's fronts beside the two Xboxes, so the HDMI switch (beside the Xbox One, where its remote reaches it) and the RetroTINK (beside the Xbox 360) move up from bay 2.
    • Bay 2's lower half becomes two columns: the sub on the left, under the TV, and the PS2 over the PS1 on the right. The sub is 21.4 × 30.4 × 29.43; its column is 23.4 wide and 35.3 tall.
    • The port: the sub's front sits flush with the face frame, so its rear port is 15.6 cm from the wall through the open back and the channel. That's inside the 15–30 cm advised for a rear port25, at the low end, so the channel behind bay 2 stays clear: Switch 2 and the retro 6-way move behind bay 1.
    • Vibration, the one thing to test: Microsoft advises keeping the Xbox 360 away from subwoofers27, and the deck shares the worktop. The 360 is a whole bay away, the sub stands on an isolation riser without touching the divider or the frame, and the deck has isolation feet. Once it's built, play a disc game and a record at film volume. If anything skips, turn the sub down for that source; if it still does, the sub can go back under the dining wall.
    • The dining wall is clear underneath: no cover to make, and nothing to move for eight at the table.

    Your plant stand and your vinyl stand

    You've bought a plant stand (98 × 29.5 × 158: two slatted towers of five tiers with an open middle holding two shelves, so taller plants fit in the middle) and you're keeping your vinyl stand (70 × 32 × 78: a black steel frame and rustic wood, two face-out bays on top, LPs standing between wire dividers below). Both are drawn from the listings you sent32,33. There are two good places for them, the window's west corner and the chimney breast (free now the table is by the stairs), so there are two layouts. In the 3D room the “Your plant stand and record shelf” buttons switch between them, and in Edit room you can drag either anywhere.

    • A, recommended: plants in the window corner, records on the breast. The plant stand stands against the window wall between the curtains' stack and the pipe boxing: 107 cm for its 98, so 4.5 each side (measure before it goes in; if it's tight, open the curtains' stack a little towards the window). Its plants get daylight from the window beside them, and at 158 it leaves 77 to the ceiling. The vinyl stand stands on the breast, centred, under the “now playing” ledge (23.6 cm clear): pick a record from its top bays, play it on the deck an arm's reach away, stand its sleeve on the ledge. About 100 more LPs.
    • B: records in the window corner, as today, plants on the breast. The plants become the breast's display, 9.75 cm clear each side; at 158 tall the stand comes up past the two frames, so the frames go up above it (or elsewhere) and the “now playing” ledge comes off.
    • Either way: your red lamp moves from the window corner to the sofa's west end; drip trays or a waterproof mat under the pots protect the slats and the carpet; felt pads under the vinyl stand.

    The vinyl is in one place, in the alcove: the deck on the worktop, the records in the two LP crates right underneath it, the preamp tucked under the shelf above, and the “now playing” ledge on the breast an arm's reach away. Pull a crate, pick a record, play it, and stand its sleeve on the ledge.

    How bay 3 works

    • Why it changed: with LPs only, v15's trays had about 10 cm of empty width each side. Now a 12 mm divider splits the bay: the LP crates take only the width LPs need, and the rest becomes a slim column that does a job.
    • The LP crates: a 33.06 cm trough, the snug width record shops use36: the sleeves stand with a little play and you flip them by their top edges. They lean back 10°; the last one leans on a raked oak rest. Outer sleeves up to 32.4 still fit.
    • Capacity: about 90 LPs per crate; two crates, about 180 LPs, the same as before.
    • The slim column: three drawers 15.26 wide, 14.06 inside. The bottom two hold DVD-size game cases face-out (13.5 wide), about 22 each, flipped like the records. The top one holds four pads on edge35, the TV, soundbar and streaming remotes, and a USB-C lead fed from the 10-gang to charge a pad in the drawer.
    • Runners: 400 mm full extension everywhere; 68–70 kg a pair under the crates. A full crate weighs about 30 kg: open one at a time, and fit the anti-tip brackets before loading.

    The turntable zone

    • The deck: on isolation feet, 2 cm back from the worktop's front edge, with 8.8 cm behind it for the lid's hinges. The zone takes a deck up to the size of an AT-LP120X (45.2 × 35.2 cm); most decks are smaller.
    • The lid: AT's cover is 44.1 × 34.6 cm17, so standing open its top edge is at about 121; the shelf's underside is at 130.
    • Bass: the sub is in bay 2, in the same base the deck sits on. It stands on an isolation riser, clear of the divider and the frame, and the deck stands on isolation feet. If a record skips or hums at film volume, turn the sub down for vinyl.
    • Signal path: turntable set to PHONO → the preamp under the shelf → a 2 m RCA-to-3.5 mm lead down the groove behind the right upright and along the back of the worktop to the soundbar's AUX. If the deck has no PHONO/LINE switch, plug it straight into the AUX.
    • Soundbar: Music mode, bass up, surround, night and dialogue modes off. Always the AUX cable, never Bluetooth.

    One oak line at 155.4 cm runs from the ledge over the TV, round the corner on the left upright, and along the side wall. The side wall's part is one run, 4 cm thick all along: a 7 cm record ledge with four more LPs face-out that sweeps out in one smooth curve to the 28 cm shelf the PC sits on, ending in a 5 cm radius like the table's corners. A warm LED strip in a groove under its front edge washes the wall below it, on the uprights' driver and dimmer. Two separate shelves at two depths become one piece of furniture, and it moves the PC out of the TV's sightlines.

    • The run: 220 cm long, 4 thick, cut from one 225 × 30 × 4 oak board to a full-size template: 7 deep along the LPs (with a 1.5 cm lip), easing out to 28 over 14 cm just past the last LP. It sits on an oak cleat screwed to the side wall, dowelled to the left upright's front edge.
    • The PC end: 82 × 28 cm, on two concealed heavy-duty brackets (40 kg+ a pair) as well as the cleat, 71.4 cm above the sofa's back. The case sits with its glass to the room and its front towards the alcove. The ports face the window and stay open to the air (no screen, so nothing traps the exhaust); from the sofa you look at the glass side, not the ports. The pad dock sits beyond the case.
    • Cables: through a brush grommet at the shelf's back corner straight into a 25 mm conduit chased into the side wall (it's solid, as you confirmed), down to skirting height and behind the skirting to the base's plinth; you chase it yourselves in step 3, with a second, smaller conduit beside it for the PC's mains lead, then it's filled and painted, so nothing shows. A draw wire left in it pulls the next lead through. The HDMI is an active optical cable (about 5 m), "source" end at the PC.
    • Power: the PC plugs into the 10-gang behind the TV: its lead (a 5 m C13 lead with a rewireable plug, fed down bare and the plug fitted at the bottom) runs in its own 25 mm conduit beside the data one. The 10-gang's load check, with the PC, is in the Network & power chapter. No new socket.
    • Keyboard tray (back from v6.1): the shelf sits on a 7 cm oak housing with a tray on 300 mm light-duty runners that rolls 25 cm out towards the room. It holds a full-size wireless keyboard and mouse: pull it out, lift the keyboard onto your lap, park it again. The housing stops 12 cm short of the sofa end so the cables drop past it; its underside is 144.4, 64.4 above the sofa's back.
    • Headroom: the shelf's underside is at 151.4, and it covers only the 28 cm of the sofa nearest the wall.
    The PC end, looked over again

    Electrics: your own job

    You're doing the electrics yourselves. In England, Part P of the Building Regulations makes only three kinds of work notifiable: a new circuit, a replacement consumer unit, and any addition or alteration to a circuit in a special location (round a bath or shower). Replacing an accessory like for like, and adding to an existing circuit anywhere else, isn't notifiable, though it must still be done to the wiring regulations (BS 7671). So the jobs here need no electrician and no building control: the socket swapped for a double, and the two spot bars in place of the old fittings (the light switches stay: the bars' smart bulbs need full power, so there are no dimmers to fit). The Cat6 and the conduits aren't mains work at all.

    The safe routine, every time
    1. Isolate: switch off that circuit's breaker at the consumer unit (the lighting circuit for the bars, the socket circuit for the socket). If the labels aren't clear, switch off the main switch.
    2. Lock off: fit the MCB lock-off and padlock, keep the key in your pocket, and tape a note on the board.
    3. Prove dead: check the tester lights on its proving unit, test between every pair of terminals (live–neutral, live–earth, neutral–earth), then check the tester on the proving unit again.
    4. Photograph the wiring before you disconnect anything, and connect the new one wire for wire: brown (or red) to L, blue (or black) to N, green-and-yellow to earth, sleeved, no copper showing, every screw tight.
    5. Test: power back on, then the socket tester in both outlets; each bar's four bulbs come on and join the app.
    Stop and call an electrician if…
    • the tester shows anything live after you've isolated;
    • the wiring is old (rubber or fabric sheath, or red and black with no earth), or there's no earth at a ceiling point (the spot bars need one);
    • there are more wires than you can match to your photo (two-way switching, a loop in a ceiling rose you can't follow), or scorch marks, or a loose, hot or crumbling fitting;
    • the consumer unit has rewireable fuses or no RCD;
    • a job grows into a new circuit, consumer unit work, or anything by the bath or shower.

    Cable routes

    • The channel: 4 cm behind the frames, flat two-compartment trunking: mains on one side, HDMI, Cat6 and audio on the other. Switch 2 and the retro 6-way stand on edge in it.
    • The groove behind the right upright: Deco B's 12 V and patch leads, the Series X's HDMI and power, and the vinyl lead, down to the worktop's slot.
    • The PC: through the shelf's brush grommet into two conduits chased into the side wall (the HDMI and Cat6 in a 38 mm one, its mains lead in a 25 mm one), behind the skirting and into the plinth notch; the mains lead goes on to the 10-gang.
    • The sub: its mains lead from the 10-gang drops through the slot behind the TV to the back of bay 2, about 1 m. Keep the channel behind the sub clear: its port needs the air.
    • Airflow: console bays stay open-backed; the Series X has 15 cm each side and 21 above.

    Network

    • Bedroom 3: the Hub 5 (in modem mode), Deco A and Switch 1 sit together with the gaming PCs. Switch 1's eight ports: the uplink, two PCs, the two Cat6 runs down to Deco B and Deco C, and, if you want them, the projector in the master and the music room in bedroom 2.
    • The route down: across the landing to the airing cupboard, which sits over the alcove's corner, and down through its floor. Run 1 comes through the living room ceiling in the alcove's right corner to Deco B; run 2 follows the right upright's groove down and through the floor to the kitchen, where Deco C goes on the outside of the brick cupboard, up high.
    • Sloped ceilings: bedroom 2 and the bathroom slope down to the back wall; keep any Deco or desk in bedroom 2 on the high side.

    What each part does

    PartWhereJobWhy it's needed
    Virgin Hub 5, in modem modeBedroom 3Brings the internet in, nothing elseTwo routers fighting (double NAT) breaks Xbox online play; its Wi-Fi switches off
    Deco A (main)Bedroom 3The router: Wi-Fi, parental controls, HomeShieldHomeShield and parental controls only work when the Deco is the router
    Switch 1, 8-portBedroom 3Turns Deco A's spare port into sevenThe two PCs, both Cat6 runs down, and the optional projector and music-room runs
    Deco BLiving room, high shelf at 196Wi-Fi for the living room, and the wired point for the wallFixes the living room's weak 5 GHz side
    Switch 2, 8-portStanding on edge in the channel behind the baseTurns Deco B's spare port into sevenThe Series X, Xbox One, Xbox 360, PS3, PC and TV each get a cable, one port spare
    Deco CKitchen, high on the outside of the brick cupboardWi-Fi for the kitchenThe kitchen gets poor signal on every band today
    Cat6 runs 1 and 2Bedroom 3 → airing cupboard → alcove corner, and on to the kitchenThe wired link between Decos ("Ethernet backhaul")Without it the Decos relay each other over the 5 GHz band the phones use, losing speed at each hop

    Stage 1: the mesh up today, before any cables

    1. Unplug everything from the hub. Log in at 192.168.0.1 with the password on its base, then Modem Mode → Enable Modem Mode → Apply. Its settings page moves to 192.168.100.1.
    2. Connect a hub port to Deco A and set it up in the Deco app, reusing the old Wi-Fi name and password. If it shows no internet, try another port and restart the hub.
    3. Plug Switch 1 into Deco A's other port, then the PCs into Switch 1.
    4. Add Deco B in the living room and Deco C in the kitchen. For now they link over Wi-Fi.
    5. Check the Xbox's network settings show NAT: Open.

    Stage 2: after your Cat6 runs (step 3)

    1. Plug run 1 into Deco B's free port (Switch 2 stays in the other) and run 2 into Deco C.
    2. In the Deco app, check Deco B and Deco C show as "Ethernet".
    3. Plug the Series X, Xbox One, Xbox 360, PS3, PC and TV into Switch 2.
    4. Under QoS, give the Series X and the PC high priority; turn on guest Wi-Fi and automatic firmware.
    Cabling rules
    • Solid pure-copper Cat6, round; not CCA or flat cable for the long runs. Measure the real route and add 2–3 m.
    • Cross mains at right angles; never staple through a cable; no kinks; label both ends. Never two cables between the same two devices.
    • Done when: Deco B and C show "Ethernet", each PC shows 1.0 Gbps, the Xbox shows NAT: Open, and phones hold a strong signal in the kitchen and across the living room.

    AV: everything sounds through the Hisense

    SourcePictureSound
    PC · Xbox Series XTV HDMI 1 · HDMI 3Via the TV over eARC (5.1 or Atmos)
    Xbox One, Xbox 360, PS3HDMI switch → TV HDMI 4Via the TV over eARC, 5.1
    PS2Component → RetroTINK → switch → TVOptical straight to the soundbar
    PS1RGB SCART → RetroTINK → switch → TVStereo through the RetroTINK and eARC
    Turntable · phone—Preamp → AUX · Bluetooth

    TV settings: rename the inputs (HDMI 4 "Retro"), Deep Colour on HDMI 1, 3 and 4, Game Optimiser on the console inputs, sound out to HDMI eARC. RetroTINK-6X CE: a 5 V 2 A USB plug on the retro 6-way; the PS2's Component Video Out set to Y Cb/Pb Cr/Pr; RGB SCART for the PS1.

    Sound layout

    • Sub: wireless, in bay 2 under the TV, its driver facing the room and its rear port 15.6 cm from the wall through the open back (15–30 is advised25). Next to the soundbar, its bass blends with the bar instead of coming from behind you, and it's off the floor where feet and drinks are. If the bass booms, turn it down rather than moving it.
    • Rears: one on the side wall at seated ear height behind the sofa's corner, one on a stand past the sofa's west end; linked by a cable behind the sofa, powered from your double socket behind the sofa's short side.

    • From your v13 message: less cladding (done: no slats, spine, sub box or reeding; cables chased into the wall); the stairs go up; the drawer layouts drawn.
    • From your answers: the sofa's long side ends in line with the breast's reveal; the door hinges on the breast side and opens in; the side wall and breast are solid (plugs and screws, no stud fixings); the PC is an average gaming case (allowed for at 23 × 45.3 × 46.6).
    • Artisan oak, Card Room Green with matching eggshell skirting, every record face-out, the game drawer as designed.
    • The TV 25.25 cm nearer the side wall, the turntable in the alcove, the Series X above it, the records below.
    • The ledge wrapping round onto the side wall, with the PC above the sofa.
    • A fold-down oak dining table on the chimney breast; the spot bars on the existing ceiling points; the sub back in the media wall, in bay 2.

    Later ideas

    • For the room: a glass display case on the breast, glass plant shelves in the window, a C-table for the sofa's open end, and small ones (TV backlight that follows the picture, cushions in the rug's colours, a plant uplight, a rug pad): see the appendix “Ideas for later”, and the Ideas tab and buttons in the 3D room.

    How the media wall's layout was chosen

    Why this layout, and what we ruled out
    • The TV in the middle: left two 25.25 cm gaps either side, too narrow for a turntable, so the vinyl had to move out to the chimney breast. Moving the TV joins them into one 50.5 cm zone.
    • The turntable with the Series X beside it: 45.2 + 20.5 cm won't go in 50.5. The Series X goes up on a shelf instead, above the lid's swing, where it gets more air than it had in v10 (15 cm each side, 21 above).
    • The vinyl cabinet on the breast as well as a table: a table needs the breast's full width, and a cabinet in front would put the diners 44 cm further into the room.
    • A gateleg table in the recess: it would block the door; the breast is the only clear wall.

    Demma Home Improvements · Portsmouth Close · living room

    constructionBuild

    0 of 13 steps done

    Tick each step when it's done; it saves for both of you. "Buy first" opens that part of the buy list.

    Show one part

    One step at a time otherwise: it opens on the first one not done.
    1. 1

      Prep

      Measure and count

      You · 2 h
      Tools
      • Tape measure
      • Spirit level, 120 cm
      • A notebook (or the questions list on the plan page)
      Read the full step expand_more
      1. The alcove's width at the floor, 76, 134, 155 and 196 cm and at the ceiling: cut everything to the smallest.
      2. The floor's level across the alcove, and the chimney breast's flatness with a long level.
      3. The door's swing, and the sofa: overall width, depth with the return, back height.
      4. Count the LPs and games (PS2, Xbox 360, Xbox One), and measure ten cases of each.
      5. Make a cardboard template of the alcove at worktop height: walls are rarely square.

      Check before moving on: Every figure within 1 cm of the plan. If not, send the numbers and the drawings are redone first.

      Also see: The room

    2. 2

      Network

      Network, stage 1

      You · 2 h

      Buy firstNetwork, now · £51–70

      Parts
      • Two TP-Link TL-SG108 8-port switches
      • Cat6 patch leads, 0.5–2 m (11)
      Tools
      • A phone with the Deco app
      • A laptop for the hub's settings page
      Drawing for this step
      Read the full step expand_more
      1. Unplug everything from the Hub 5. Log in at 192.168.0.1 with the password on its base, then Modem Mode → Enable Modem Mode → Apply. Its page moves to 192.168.100.1.
      2. Connect a hub port to Deco A in bedroom 3 and set it up in the Deco app, reusing the old Wi-Fi name and password. If it shows no internet, try another hub port and restart the hub.
      3. Plug the new 8-port Switch 1 into Deco A's other port, then the PCs into Switch 1.
      4. Add Deco B in the living room and Deco C in the kitchen. For now they link over Wi-Fi.
      5. Speed-test each room, and check the Xbox's network settings show NAT: Open.

      Check before moving on: Internet in every room, and NAT: Open on the Xbox.

      Also see: Network

    3. 3

      Power & cablesNetwork

      Cables and the socket, your own job

      You + a helper · 2–3 days

      Buy firstCables and power · £265–545

      Parts
      • Cat6 solid pure copper (not CCA), 2–4 runs
      • RJ45 keystones and two surface boxes, or RJ45 plugs
      • A double socket in the same finish, and a deeper back box if the old one is shallow
      • Conduit: 38 mm and 25 mm oval, about 4 m each, two draw wires
      • A 5 m C13 lead with a rewireable 13 A plug, for the PC
      • One-coat filler
      Hardware and fixings
      • Cable clips for the Cat6 in the loft space or under the boards
      • Brown wall plugs and 4 × 30 screws for the conduit clips
      Tools
      • Two-pole voltage tester (GS38) and its proving unit
      • MCB lock-off and padlock
      • Plug-in socket tester
      • Insulated screwdrivers, wire strippers, side cutters
      • Cat6 punch-down tool (or crimper) and a cable tester
      • Draw rods
      • Wall chaser with dust extraction, or a bolster and club hammer
      • Cable and pipe detector
      • SDS drill
      • Safety glasses, ear defenders, FFP2 masks
      • A helper
      Drawings for this step
      Read the full step expand_more
      Before you start: the stop list
      1. Stop and call an electrician if: the tester shows anything live after you've isolated; the wiring is old (rubber or fabric sheath, or red and black with no earth); there are more wires than you can match to your photo; there are scorch marks or the old socket is loose or hot; the consumer unit has rewireable fuses or no RCD; or the job grows into a new circuit.
      2. Nothing in this step is notifiable in England: the socket is a like-for-like swap on an existing circuit, outside a bathroom. It must still be done to the wiring regulations, which is what this routine is for.
      The Cat6 runs (low voltage: no isolation needed)
      1. Measure each route on the house plan and add 2–3 m: bedroom 3, across the landing, down through the airing cupboard.
      2. Lift a floorboard in the airing cupboard. Drill a 20 mm hole through the plate below (detector first), and feed a draw rod down to the alcove's right corner. Tape both Cat6 cables and a spare to it and pull them through. Pull the kitchen run on down the same way, past the right upright's groove.
      3. Keep the Cat6 away from mains: cross at right angles, never run alongside in the same hole. Clip it every 30 cm; never staple through it or kink it.
      4. Punch each end down onto a keystone in a surface box (or crimp a plug), to the T568B colours on both ends. Label both ends.
      5. Test each run with the cable tester: all eight lights in order. Re-terminate any that don't.
      Isolate the socket circuit
      1. Tell everyone in the house you're working on the electrics.
      2. At the consumer unit, switch off the breaker for the side-wall socket's circuit (usually a ring marked "sockets"). If the labels aren't clear, switch off the main switch instead.
      3. Fit the MCB lock-off and padlock to that breaker, keep the key in your pocket, and tape a note on the board: "Working on this circuit, do not switch on".
      4. Prove your voltage tester on its proving unit: it must light.
      5. At the socket, with it pulled forward on its cables, test between every pair: live and neutral, live and earth, neutral and earth. No reading on any of them.
      6. Prove the tester on the proving unit again. Only now is it safe to touch.
      Swap the single socket for a double
      1. Unscrew the old socket and ease it out. Photograph the wiring before you undo anything.
      2. Check the stop list against what you see: an earth (green-and-yellow) wire present and sleeved, no scorching, the cable sheath into the box.
      3. If the double needs a bigger box, chop the plaster out round the old box to the new box's outline and fit the new box with plugs and screws, the cables through its grommets.
      4. Connect wire for wire: brown (or red) to L, blue (or black) to N, green-and-yellow to the earth terminal. Two cables in the old box go into the same terminals together. Strip only enough so no copper shows outside a terminal, and tighten every screw firmly.
      5. Fold the cables in neatly without trapping them, and screw the socket on level.
      6. Remove the lock-off, switch on, and plug the socket tester into each outlet: it should show correct wiring on both.
      The PC's two conduits in the side wall
      1. Mark the route from behind the PC shelf's back corner straight down to skirting height, then along behind the skirting to the base's plinth. Run the detector along it: move it if anything shows. Never chase near the socket's cables, which run straight up, down or across from it.
      2. Chase two channels side by side, 5 cm apart: one for the 38 mm oval conduit (data: HDMI and Cat6), one for the 25 mm (the PC's mains lead). Vertical only on the wall, no deeper than the conduit needs. Wear the mask: the dust is silica.
      3. Take the skirting off along the route, fix both conduits with a draw wire inside each, and refit the skirting over them.
      4. Fill the chase with one-coat filler, sand flush, and photograph the route with a tape measure in the shot before you paint.
      Finish
      1. Mark every route on the plan, and keep the photos with it.

      Check before moving on: The socket tester shows correct wiring on both outlets, both Cat6 runs test good end to end, and every route is photographed.

      Also see: Electrics: your own job · Power and cables

      Prep

      Mark the heights

      You · 1 h
      Tools
      • Cross-line laser level
      • Tape measure
      • Pencil and masking tape
      • Cable and pipe detector
      • Spirit level, 120 cm
      Drawing for this step
      Read the full step expand_more
      Set up a datum
      1. Find the floor's highest point across the alcove (you measured its level in step 1). Every height in this plan is measured from there.
      2. Stand the laser in the middle of the room, level it, and mark a line at exactly 100 cm above that high point on the alcove's back wall, both side walls and the chimney breast.
      3. Measure every other height up or down from the 100 line, not up from the floor: the floor is the thing that isn't level.
      The alcove's heights
      1. Put a strip of masking tape down each side wall and the back wall of the alcove and mark these heights on it:
      2. 73: the tops of the frames and bay 3 (the worktop's underside).
      3. 76: the worktop's top.
      4. 130 and 134: the Series X shelf, underside and top.
      5. 153 and 155.4: the record ledge and the wrap ledge, underside and top.
      6. 192 and 196: the high shelf, underside and top.
      7. Carry the 153 and 155.4 lines along the side wall to 250 cm out from the alcove's back wall, for the wrap ledge and the PC shelf.
      Across the back wall
      1. Mark the uprights' positions from the side wall: the left one 0–4.5, the right one 131–135.5. Turn the laser to its vertical line and draw both lines from the worktop line to the ceiling.
      2. Mark the base from the side wall along the floor: filler 0–3, bay 1 3–63, bay 2 63–123, bay 3 123–183, filler to 186.
      On the chimney breast
      1. Find the breast's centre: 58.75 cm from its alcove-side corner. Draw it plumb from the floor to 170.
      2. Mark the backboard: 55 cm either side of the centre line, from 51.3 to 73.3 high.
      3. Mark the two bracket centres 40 cm either side of the centre line.
      4. Mark the folded table's top edge at 153.3, and the framed LPs' bottom edges at 165.
      Check for cables
      1. Run the detector along every line where you'll drill: the cleats, the spacer blocks, the upright brackets, the backboard and the PC shelf.
      2. Mark anything it finds in red, and compare with your own photos from step 3. Move a fixing 5 cm rather than drill near a cable.

      Check before moving on: Every line level end to end, and the uprights' lines plumb.

      Build the base

      You · 1 day

      Buy firstBase unit · £457–892

      Parts
      • Two IKEA BESTÅ frames 60 × 40 × 64
      • 18 mm birch ply: bay 3 sides 73 × 40 (2), top and bottom 56.4 × 40 (2); plinth rails 120 × 9 (2), cross-pieces 34.4 × 9 (3)
      • Four 4 cm spacer blocks (ply offcuts, 4 × 10 × 1.8)
      • Anti-tip brackets: two per bay (6)

      • Plastic shims
      • Four connector bolts (furniture joint connectors)
      Hardware and fixings
      • 4 × 40 and 4 × 50 mm wood screws
      • 5 × 60 mm screws and brown wall plugs

      Tools

      • Spirit level, 60 and 120 cm
      • Combination square
      • Clamps

      Drawings for this step
      Read the full step expand_more
      The plinth under bays 1 and 2
      1. Lay the two 120 × 9 rails on edge, 38 cm apart outside, and stand the three 34.4 × 9 cross-pieces between them: one at each end and one in the middle, at 60.
      2. Pre-drill, glue and screw through the rails into each cross-piece end with two 4 × 40 screws.
      3. Measure both diagonals: when they're equal the frame is square. The plinth is 120 × 38 × 9. The opening between 60 and 120 stays clear: it's the hidden drawer's bay.
      4. Stand it in the alcove 3 cm from the side wall and 4 cm off the back wall. Level it with shims, side to side and front to back.
      The BESTÅ frames
      1. Assemble both frames to IKEA's instructions, but leave the back panels off: the open backs are how the cables and the sub's port breathe.
      2. Join the two frames side by side with IKEA's connectors.
      3. Stand them on the plinth, their backs flush with its back edge, so their fronts sit 2 cm proud of the plinth (the face frame covers the step).
      Bay 3, the carcass for the LP crates and the slim column
      1. While the sides are flat, mark the runner lines on their inner faces: on the right side 2.3 and 37.0 cm up from the bottom edge, for the two LP crates; on the left side 2.3, 25.1 and 47.9, for the three slim drawers.
      2. Stand the bottom panel between the two sides, flush with their bottom edges, and the top panel flush with their top edges. Pre-drill, countersink, glue and screw with four 4 × 50 screws a joint.
      3. Check the diagonals for square. The carcass is 60 × 40 × 73, open at the back.
      4. Stand it in its place, 123–183 from the side wall, its top level with the frames' tops at 73. Shim under it if the floor drops away.
      5. Clamp it to bay 2 and fit two connector bolts at the front and two at the back.
      Fix it to the wall
      1. Screw a 4 cm spacer block to the back wall behind the top of each bay, at 68 high, with plugs.
      2. Push the whole base back against the blocks.
      3. Fit two anti-tip brackets per bay through the blocks into the wall. Do this before anything heavy goes in: a full LP crate pulled out is about 30 kg in front of the unit.
      4. Lay a level across all three tops: within 1 mm over 186 cm. Shim and re-check.
      The cable channel
      1. Lay the flat two-compartment trunking on the floor in the 4 cm channel behind the base: mains on the wall side, data on the other.
      2. Run the leads in now: the two mains leads from the side-wall socket enter through the plinth's left end, the Cat6 and Deco B's lead come down the right-hand corner.
      3. Keep the channel behind bay 2 empty: the sub's port breathes into it. Switch 2 and the retro 6-way stand on edge behind bay 1.

      Check before moving on: The tops level within 1 mm across 186 cm, and nothing rocks.

      Media wall

      Fit the worktop

      You + a helper · ½ day

      Buy firstOak joinery · £745–1,355

      Parts
      • One solid oak worktop, 300 × 62 × 3, full stave
      • A 60 mm brush strip and a 35 mm brush grommet
      Hardware and fixings
      • 4 × 30 mm screws with washers (9)
      • Hardwax oil
      Tools
      • Hardboard or cardboard, 190 × 50, for the template
      • Compass or a pencil on a block, for scribing
      • Track saw or circular saw with a guide
      • Jigsaw
      • Router with a straight bit
      • Random-orbit sander, 120 and 180 grit
      • Drill-driver
      • A helper
      Drawing for this step
      Read the full step expand_more
      Make a template
      1. Cut the hardboard to about 190 × 50 and push it into the alcove at worktop height, its back edge against the back wall.
      2. Set the compass to the widest gap at one end and run it down the side wall, so the pencil copies the wall's line onto the board. Cut to the line. Do the other end the same way.
      3. Mark the front edge at 46 cm from the back wall all along. The template is now the worktop's exact shape.
      Cut the oak
      1. Lay the board best face up, grain running along its length. Lay the template on it and draw round it.
      2. Cut just outside the line with the track saw, then sand or plane to the line.
      3. From the offcut, cut the dining wall's backboard: 110 × 22 × 10.3.
      4. Chamfer the worktop's top front edge with a 3 mm chamfer, sanded by hand.
      Cut the openings
      1. The TV slot: 3 cm wide, from 1 to 4 cm in from the back edge, running 27.75–107.75 from the side wall. Clamp a batten as a guide and rout it in passes, or drill each end and jigsaw between. Push the brush strip in.
      2. The grommet hole behind the deck: 35 mm, its centre 2.5 cm from the back edge and 160.75 from the side wall.
      Finish and fix
      1. Sand to 120, then 180. Oil every face: top, underside, both ends and the cut edges of the slot. Two coats, a night between them.
      2. Two of you lift it in and push it back to the wall. It should touch both side walls along their length.
      3. Inside each bay, drill three 5 mm holes up through the top panel, elongated front to back to about 12 mm long, so the oak can move with the seasons.
      4. Screw up through them into the worktop with 4 × 30 screws and washers. They must not come out through the top: check the length against a scrap.

      Check before moving on: Tight to both walls, and the slot sits over the channel.

      Drawings for this step
      Read the full step expand_more
      The console shelves
      1. Bay 1, from the top: rows of 16 (Xbox One), 16 (Xbox 360), then the game drawer's 25.2. Put the shelves on the pin holes nearest those heights.
      2. Bay 2: the PS3's row of 23.7 at the top, on a full-width shelf. Below it, the PS2 and the PS1 sit beside the sub (next part).
      Bay 2's sub column
      1. Stand the 12 mm divider on the bay's floor, 23.4 cm from the bay's left inner face, tight under the PS3 shelf. Check it's plumb.
      2. Fix it with one small angle bracket at the bottom (into the frame's bottom panel) and one at the top (into the PS3 shelf's underside).
      3. Drill two 5 mm pin holes in the divider's right face at the height of the frame's pin holes for the PS2/PS1 shelf. Fit the part shelf on four pins.
      4. Pair the sub with the soundbar now: its PAIR button is on the back, and it's hard to reach once it's in.
      5. Lay the isolation riser on the column's floor, its front edge flush with the frame's front.
      6. Stand the sub on it with the grille facing the room, centred: 1 cm to the divider, 1 cm to the frame's side. Slide it forward until its front is flush with the face frame's front (2 cm proud of the frame). Run its lead out of the back.
      7. Check it touches nothing but the riser. If it does, a sheet of felt between, or nudge it.
      The game drawer (bay 1, bottom row)
      1. Fit the 350 mm runners to the frame's sides, level, so the drawer's base will sit about 1 cm above the frame's bottom panel. Drill pilot holes: BESTÅ sides are particleboard. If a screw won't hold, glue a 12 mm ply packer behind the runner.

      4. Fit the cross divider 13 cm back from the front, and the two bin walls 16 cm in from each side. Glue in the bin floors with a slight back-rake, so the cases lean about 13°.
      5. Felt the base and make the follower blocks.
      6. Fit the runners' inner members to the box, hang it, and check it runs true empty.
      Bay 3: the divider, the LP crates and the slim drawers
      1. Stand the 12 mm divider in the bay, its left face 17.8 cm from the left side's inner face, the full height inside. Check it's plumb and parallel to the side at front and back (measure both), then fix it with two small angle brackets top and bottom.
      2. Mark the runner lines on the divider's faces: on its right face 2.3 and 37.0 (the crates), on its left face 2.3, 25.1 and 47.9 (the slim drawers), matching the lines on the sides.
      3. Screw the crates' 400 mm runners to the right side and the divider's right face; the slim drawers' to the left side and the divider's left face. Use every hole: a full crate is about 30 kg.
      4. For each LP crate, glue and pin the two 40 × 8 sides and two 33.1 × 8 ends on top of the 34.9 × 40 base. The trough is 33 inside: snug for 31.4 sleeves, like a record shop's crate.
      5. Glue a raked rest (an oak offcut) at the back of each crate, so the sleeves lean back about 10°. Felt the trough.
      6. For each slim drawer, glue and pin the 6 mm sides, back and front onto the 15.3 × 40 base: 14.1 inside, for 13.5 cm game cases face-out. In the top one, glue a 6 mm strip down the middle (two pads on edge each side) and drill a 20 mm hole in the back for the USB-C lead's grommet.

      1. Make the box: the two 34 × 4.4 sides, the two 49.6 × 4.4 ends between them, the 6 mm base screwed underneath. It's 52 × 34 × 5.
      2. Pack the plinth's inner faces under bay 2 with ply strips so the 300 mm runners sit the box's width plus their allowance apart, and fit the runners with the box 1.6 cm off the floor.
      3. Felt the runners: the drawer sits under the sub.

      1. Cut the stiles (about 5 wide, and one 2 wide over bay 3's divider) and the rails from 2 cm oak. The bottom rail covers the plinth, 9 tall under bays 1–2, with an opening 54 × 6 for the plinth drawer, 1.6 up, under bay 2.

      Read the full step expand_more
      Cut the uprights to length
      1. Measure from the worktop to the ceiling at each upright's position. The plan says 159; ceilings vary.
      2. Cut each upright 2 mm under its measurement, then scribe its top to the ceiling as you did the worktop.
      3. Mark each upright's faces: which side faces the TV, and the back edge that goes against the wall.
      The housings (both uprights)
      1. Measure from each upright's foot (the end on the worktop). The high shelf's housing is 116–120 up, the full 30 depth, 1.2 deep, on the TV-side face of both uprights.
      2. The record ledge's housing is 77–79.4 up, 0–7 from the back edge, 1.2 deep, on the TV-side face of both.
      3. On the right upright's other face (the turntable side), a second high shelf housing at 116–120, full depth, for the short length.
      4. Clamp a straight batten as a guide, set the router 4 mm deep and rout, then step down to 12 mm in passes. Square the ends with a chisel. Practise on an offcut first.
      The through-mortises (right upright)
      1. Two mortises, each 6 wide and 2.4 tall, at 54.8–57.2 up from the foot, 12–18 and 20–26 cm from the back edge.
      2. Mark them on both faces with a square and a knife. Drill most of each out with the 20 mm bit, halfway from each face, then chisel to the lines.
      3. On the TV-side face, flare the top and bottom of each mortise outwards 3–4 mm, for the wedges.
      The tenons (Series X shelf)
      1. On the shelf's west end (the end that goes through the upright), mark two tenons 6 wide and 2.4 thick, centred in its 4 cm thickness, 12–18 and 20–26 from its back edge, 4.5 long.
      2. Saw the shoulders and cheeks, and cut away the rest of the end back to the shoulder line.
      3. Saw a kerf 3 cm deep across the middle of each tenon, parallel to the shelf's faces.
      4. Test-fit through the mortises: snug, pushed in by hand.
      The grooves
      1. On each upright's TV-side face, rout a groove for the LED channel (usually about 1.7 wide × 0.8 deep: check yours), 2 cm in from the front edge, from 2 cm above the worktop to just under the high shelf's housing.
      2. On the right upright's back edge, rout a 2 × 1.5 cable groove the full length, for Deco B's 12 V and patch leads, the Series X's HDMI and power, and the vinyl lead.
      3. Notch both uprights' tops for the ceiling LED strip.
      Dry-fit, then fix
      1. Lay each upright on the floor with its shelves in their housings. Check every joint closes before any glue.
      2. Drill two 10 mm holes 3 cm deep in each upright's foot, and matching holes in the worktop at the marked positions (dowel centres make this exact). Glue the dowels into the uprights only, so they can come out.
      3. Lay Deco B's leads and the other cables into the right upright's back groove.
      4. Stand the left upright on its dowels against the side wall. Screw it to the side wall through three countersunk holes, with plugs, and plug the holes with oak.
      5. Stand the right upright on its dowels, check it's plumb with the laser, and fix it to the back wall with the concealed brackets.
      6. Slide the long high shelf and the record ledge into their housings from the front.
      7. Screw a 30 cm cleat to the breast's side face (the reveal) for the short high shelf, and another at the Series X shelf's underside height. Slide the short high shelf in from the front onto its cleat and into its housing.
      8. Feed the Series X shelf's tenons through the mortises from the turntable side, onto its cleat. Glue the wedges and drive them into the kerfs from the TV side. When dry, saw them flush and plane: proud, they'd touch the TV.
      9. Pegs: drill 10 mm through each upright's face into the housed shelf ends, 4 cm deep, about 4 cm from the front edge. Glue in a peg and saw it flush.
      The “now playing” ledge on the breast
      1. Cut it 105.5 × 7 × 2.4 from the shelf board's offcut and glue a 1.5 cm lip along its front edge, so a sleeve stands against the wall without sliding.
      2. Mark a level line on the chimney breast at 101.6 (the ledge's underside), 6 cm in from each side of the breast.
      3. Fit its two concealed brackets to the maker's instructions, slide the ledge on, and stand three LPs on it.

      Check before moving on: Uprights plumb, shelves level, the TV slides in with 2 cm each side, and the “now playing” ledge is level with an LP standing on it.

      1. Fit the concealed brackets into the wall at the shelf's height, through the cleat, to the maker's instructions.
      2. Cut the grommet hole in the shelf's back corner, over the top of the chased conduit.
      3. Screw the keyboard tray's housing to the shelf's underside, stopping 12 cm short of the sofa end so the cables drop past it. Fit the runners inside it and slide the tray in.
      4. Slide the shelf onto its brackets and down onto the cleat. Lean on it: it shouldn't move.
      The PC's leads
      1. Fit the brush grommet. Pull the HDMI (active optical: the end marked "source" at the PC) and the Cat6 down the 38 mm conduit with its draw wire.
      2. Take the plug off the C13 lead, feed its bare end down the 25 mm conduit, and at the bottom fit the rewireable plug: brown to L, blue to N, green-and-yellow to E, the cord grip on the outer sheath, a 13 A fuse.
      3. At the bottom, all three run behind the skirting into the plinth's notch and the channel; the mains lead goes on to the 10-gang behind the TV.
      The PC's extras
      1. Screw the powered USB hub under the side run's front edge, below the PC, ports facing the sofa. Its adapter plugs into the 10-gang along the PC's mains route; its lead runs up through the grommet to the PC.
      2. Remote power button: with the PC unplugged, push the receiver card into a spare slot and plug its lead onto the motherboard's power-switch pins (the case's own button lead plugs into the card's pass-through). Stick the push button to the wrap ledge's underside, by the sofa end.
      3. Lay the magnetic dust filter on the PC's top exhaust; brush it off once a month.

      Check before moving on: One level line with the ledge over the TV, the sweep runs smooth with no flat spots, and the PC end holds your weight leaning on it.

      Drawings for this step
      Read the full step expand_more
      Order the oak
      1. Ask the timber merchant for two centre panels as edge-glued staves, 101 × 80 × 2.7 each: 96 between the shoulders plus a 2.5 tongue at each end. Most will also cut the four breadboard ends and radius the half's two free corners.
      The breadboard ends (both panels)
      1. On each end of each centre panel, rout a tongue 2.5 long and 0.9 thick, centred in its thickness: take 0.9 off each face with the router against a batten.
      2. In each breadboard end's inner edge, rout a groove 0.9 wide and 2.6 deep, centred, full length.
      3. Dry-fit: the breadboard ends flush with the panel's long edges, flat across the joint.
      4. Drill three 10 mm peg holes down through each breadboard end and the tongue in it: one at the centre and one 8 cm in from each long edge, 1.3 cm from the breadboard's inner edge.
      5. Take the ends off. Elongate the two outer holes in each tongue to 16 mm long, along the panel's width: the panel moves with the seasons, the breadboard doesn't.
      6. Glue only the middle 10 cm of each tongue and groove, clamp the ends on, and drive the pegs. Glue the outer pegs into the breadboard only, not the tongue. Saw flush and sand.
      Shape and finish
      1. Radius the half's two free corners to 5 cm (the top's corners meet the wall and the half, so they stay square): jigsaw outside the line, then sand to it.
      2. Chamfer the underside edges 1 cm, except the two that meet at the joint, so it reads slim.
      3. Sand both to 180. Oil both faces of both panels equally, every edge too: a panel oiled on one side cups.
      The joint: three flip-top hinges
      1. Lay the top and the half face up, their meeting edges together, flush across the top. Mark three hinges: one in the middle and one 15 cm in from each side.
      2. Each hinge's two leaves set into the two edges; rout the recesses to the hinge's depth with a guide, square them with a chisel, and screw the hinges in. The pin sits so the half swings over onto the top through 180° and lies flat on it.
      3. Swing it: open, the two tops are flush; folded, the half lies flat on the top with nothing proud.
      The gate leg
      1. Tenon the two legs into the ends of the apron, the legs 8 cm in from the half's sides, square. Glue and clamp.
      2. Screw the two butt hinges along the apron's top edge and up into the half's underside, 3 cm in from its far edge, so the gate swings down to stand upright and up to lie flat along the half's 80 cm.
      3. Fit a folding locking stay from each leg to the half's underside: upright, they lock; push the knuckle to fold.
      4. Stand it on the floor upside down and check: folded, the legs lie flat with 1.5 cm to spare before the joint.
      The backboard and hinge rail
      1. First, knock along the stairs wall where the backboard goes. A solid sound: brick, so plugs and screws as below. A hollow sound: plasterboard on studs. Then stop and find the studs with a detector before drilling anything; the screws go into the studs (or the fixings change), so tell us what you find.
      2. Glue and screw the hinge rail along the backboard's top edge, flush at the back, so it stands 7.3 cm proud of the backboard's face.
      3. Hold the backboard on its marks: centred on the wall, the rail's top at 73.3, level.
      4. Drill through it and into the wall every 20 cm in two rows, 3 cm from its top and bottom edges. Plug, then fix with 5 × 70 countersunk screws.
      The brackets
      1. Screw the two Hebgo brackets to the backboard's face, 80 cm apart centre to centre (15 cm in from each end), their arm tops level with the rail's top.
      2. Use long screws through the backboard into plugs in the wall, as many as the bracket's holes take: the 500 kg rating depends on the fixing.
      3. Raise both arms until they click and lock. Lay a level across them.
      Hang the table
      1. Screw the three lift-off hinges along the rail's front edge, 10 cm from each end and one in the middle, pin halves on the rail.
      2. Screw the other halves to the underside of the top's back edge (the long edge that meets the wall) at the same spacing, all the same hand.
      3. With your helper, lower the top onto the pins and let it rest on the arms: at 76, level, in line with the alcove's worktop.
      4. Flip the half out and lower its gate leg: it should stand level with the top all along. Adjust with felt glides if the floor isn't flat.
      Folded
      1. Fold the gate flat, flip the half back over onto the top, then lift the pair to vertical together: two people, one at each corner (about 37 kg).
      2. Its top edge is at 153.3. Screw the two oak turn buttons to the wall just above it, 15 cm in from each end. Fit the magnetic catch behind the top edge.
      3. Open and fold it three times: it shouldn't bind, both arms should click, the gate's stays should lock, and nothing should move when you lean on it open.

      Check before moving on: It opens onto both brackets with a click each side, the half flips out flush and its gate leg locks upright; it folds back flat and swings up to the wall without binding, and nothing moves when you lean on it open.

      Lighting: smart spot bars and the LED strips, your own job

      You + a helper · 1 day

      Buy firstLighting · £288–795

      Parts
      • Both Wolston-style spot bars and eight smart colour E14 bulbs under 6 W (WiZ Colour P45 4.9 W, or Hue E14 lustre 5.1 W)
      • Smart colour strip, RGB and tunable white (about 4.5 m: Hue Lightstrip Plus or WiZ, in the bulbs' app), three aluminium channels with opal diffusers, its plug-in power
      • 6500K bias light for the TV
      • Your red lamp, with its colour bulbs
      Hardware and fixings

      Tools

      • Insulated screwdrivers, wire strippers
      • Step ladder
      • A helper to hold the bar
      Read the full step expand_more
      Before you start
      1. No dimmers: smart bulbs need full power, so leave the light switches as they are and keep them on. A dimmer in front of a smart bulb makes it flicker and can damage it.
      2. The same stop list as step 3. Here, also stop if a ceiling point has no earth (the bars need one), or the rose has more wires than you can match to your photo.
      Isolate the lighting circuit
      1. Tell everyone in the house you're working on the electrics.
      2. At the consumer unit, switch off the breaker for the lighting circuit (usually marked "lights", 6 A). If the labels aren't clear, switch off the main switch instead.
      3. Fit the MCB lock-off and padlock to that breaker, keep the key in your pocket, and tape a note on the board: "Working on this circuit, do not switch on".
      4. Prove your voltage tester on its proving unit: it must light.
      5. At each switch and each ceiling point, with the cover off, test between every pair: live and neutral, live and earth, neutral and earth. No reading on any of them.
      6. Prove the tester on the proving unit again. Only now is it safe to touch.
      Take down the old fittings, hang the bars
      1. Unscrew each old fitting's cover. Prove dead again at its terminals. Photograph the wiring, mark the switched live (the wire from the switch) with tape, then disconnect and take the fitting down.
      2. Fix bar 1's mounting plate to the ceiling over the rose between the TV and the sofa, the bar running from the TV towards the window, with screws into the joist or the plate's fixings. Bar 2's goes on the pendant point by the stairs, running the same way, along the west wall.
      3. Connect earth first (green-and-yellow to the bar's earth), then neutral to N and the switched live to L, in the bar's terminal block; any loop wires go back together exactly as they were. Tighten, tuck, and fit the canopy.
      4. Fit the smart colour bulbs and point every head straight down, evenly spread along the bar. Tilt one only if its pool lands in the TV's screen or someone's eyes. If a WiZ bulb shows below its shade's rim, use the shorter Hue lustre there.
      Power on and test
      1. Remove the lock-off and switch on, wall switches on. In the bulbs' app, add all eight, group them as bar 1 and bar 2, set warm white at about half, then save the three presets, Bright, Cosy and Film, from the lighting presets below (levels, and colours if you want them). Your red lamp's colour bulbs go in the same presets. With the table open, bar 2 comes up to at least 80 and bar 1 down to 15 (the table rule): save that as a fourth scene, Table, if your app can't do it on its own.
      The low-voltage lights (nothing to isolate)
      1. Cut the smart strip at its marks into three lengths: one for each upright's groove and one for the side-wall run. Press each into its aluminium channel under the opal diffuser; take the uprights' leads down their grooves to the strip's power on the 10-gang (smart colour).
      2. The side-wall run's strip: in its channel in the groove under the run's front edge, 1.5 cm back from the edge, the full 220 cm; its lead drops with the PC's through the brush grommet into the conduit, to the same power.
      3. Add the strips to the app beside the bars' bulbs, so each preset sets the wall's glow too: warm white for Bright, low and coloured for Cosy and Film.
      4. Clip the ceiling strip through its notches in the uprights; stick the bias light round the back of the TV on its USB port.
      5. Stand your red lamp in its spot (the 3D room shows the three), its bulbs green, pink and purple, top to bottom.

      Check before moving on: Every bulb answers the app, the presets recall, and from the sofa no spot head shows in the screen or shines in your eyes.

    Before you start: how the guide works, time, tools, techniques and pitfalls

    For anyone who's hung shelves and built flat-pack but not cut a joint. Each step: what to do, what to check, and how long it takes. Steps 3 and 12 are the electrics, with the point to stop and call an electrician. Finished sizes, in cm.

    Before you start: five rules
    • Check every wall before you drill. Run the cable and pipe detector over the spot, and never drill straight above, below or beside a socket or switch: cables run vertically and horizontally from them.
    • Measure twice, mark once, cut once. Walls are rarely square: measure the alcove at the floor, 76, 134, 155, 196 and the ceiling, and cut to the smallest.
    • Two people for anything over 15 kg: the uprights, the worktop, the table top, the TV.
    • The electrics are yours, within limits. Swapping the socket for a double and the two ceiling fittings are like-for-like jobs, not notifiable under Part P in England, as long as they meet the wiring regulations. Isolate, lock off and prove dead every time. Anything new (a new circuit, the consumer unit, work by a bath or shower) is an electrician's, and so is anything on the stop list in section 9.
    • Dry-fit everything (assemble without glue or screws) before the final fix.

    Roughly 14–18 working days spread over a few weekends, the electrics and the Cat6 included, plus the paint drying. Steps 6–11 can be split: the base and dining wall first, the oak joinery once you're confident.

    Tools

    You don't need a workshop. Hire the two big tools for a weekend (a track saw and an SDS drill), or ask the timber merchant to cut the oak and ply to the cut lists: most will, for a small charge, and that removes the hardest cuts.

    Six techniques you'll use

    1. Fixing into brick. Detect, mark, drill with the SDS on hammer setting, clear the dust, push in a brown (7 mm) wall plug and drive a 5 × 60 mm screw. In plasterboard, find a stud, or use heavy-duty plasterboard fixings rated for the load.
    2. Cutting oak cleanly. Put masking tape over the cut line, score it with a knife, cut with the good face down (circular or track saw) or up (jigsaw). Clamp a straight edge as a guide.
    3. Routing a housing (a shallow slot a shelf sits in). Clamp a straight batten as a guide, set the bit 4 mm deep, rout, then step down to 12 mm in passes. Practise on an offcut first.
    4. A wedged through-tenon. Mark the 6 × 2.4 cm mortise on both faces of the upright and drill most of it out with a 20 mm bit from each side. Chisel it to the line. Saw the tenon on the shelf's end. Saw a kerf down its middle, glue it, tap it home, then drive a glued oak wedge into the kerf. When it's dry, saw it flush and plane it.
    5. Dowelling. Use a dowel jig to drill matching 10 mm holes 3 cm deep in both parts, glue the dowels, clamp.
    6. Oiling. Sand to 180 grit, wipe off the dust, rub on a thin coat of hardwax oil, wipe off the excess after 15 minutes, let it dry overnight, give it a second coat. Do the undersides too, so the boards don't cup.

    Where beginners usually go wrong

    • Cutting the worktop to the tape instead of to a template. Make a cardboard template of the alcove first; walls are rarely square.
    • Skipping the dry-fit. Gluing a tenon that doesn't fit is the one mistake you can't undo.
    • Oil on one side only. The board cups within a week.
    • Loading the LP crates before the anti-tip brackets go in. A full crate weighs about 30 kg.
    • Folding the table up with something on it. Clear it first, every time, and keep both turn buttons turned when it's up.

    forumAsk

    16 things only you can tell us, the ones that change the drawings first. Tap an answer; a photo is often quicker than words.

    0 of 16 answered

    Answers can't be saved for both of you from this view: they're kept on this device. When you're done, use Copy all answers and paste them into a message.

    You can read the answers here but not change them. Ask Emma to give you Contributor access in the Share menu.

    • 01The stairs wall under your shelf: solid, or plasterboard on studs?

      Why we ask

      The table goes there now (the default): its brackets are rated 500 kg a pair, and the fixings depend on the wall.

      How: Knock along it: a hollow sound is plasterboard. Or look at how the shelf is fixed.

    • 02The electrics: are you swapping the two light fittings and the socket yourselves?

      Why we ask

      The plan has both as your own job (like for like, not notifiable), with the safe routine and the stop list. There are no dimmers to fit: the bars take smart bulbs. If you'd rather an electrician did the fittings, say so and we'll add that visit back.

      How: Yes, all ours; or: an electrician for the fittings only.

    • 03Your L-sofa's return: how far does it run along the side wall?

      Return along the side wall

      Why we ask

      The long side is about 266 from your photo; the return, with its open ottoman-style end towards the TV, is drawn at 168, the sofa standing 13 off the window wall. It sets the PC shelf, the walkway and the dining clearances.

      How: Overall depth with the return, from the window wall; back height and seat depth too if you can.

    • 04The stairs wall's sizes: its length, and where your shelf sits on it

      Shelf top

      Why we ask

      Your photos give about 257–268 cm from the stair box to the window corner, the shelf starting about 41 cm from the stairs; it's drawn stopping 2 short of the pipe boxing, its top at 196. Your OBEGRÄNSAD (36 tall) only stands on it under the 235 ceiling if the top is 198 or lower. The table under it is drawn from these.

      How: Tape along the wall at floor level; the shelf's two ends from the corner, and its height from the floor.

    • 05The turntable's make and model, and does it have a PHONO/LINE switch?

      PHONO/LINE switch

      Why we ask

      The zone takes up to 45.2 × 35.2 cm; the switch decides whether you need the separate preamp.

      How: The model is usually on the plinth or underneath.

    • 06The Series X fan stand's make and model

      Its width

      Why we ask

      The shelf takes a footprint up to about 30 cm wide; the plan assumes 20.5 × 20.5.

      How: A photo of the stand is enough.

    • 07Keeping the chairs: which of the ways?

      Cupboard
      Behind the top
      Fold-down seat

      Why we ask

      The plan is the chair cupboard beside the table: four folded chairs at 22 deep, flush with the pipe boxing, or six at 31 deep (9 cm proud). New: four more can hang behind the folded top (the table then stands 22 cm further out), and a fold-down seat can go in the gap at the stair end. Under the stairs is brick, so the garage is the other place.

      How: Four or six in the cupboard; and yes or no to behind the top and to the fold-down seat.

    • 08Your sofa's ottoman: how tall is it?

      Height

      Why we ask

      Drawn 75 cm square (one seat of the sofa, as you said) and 44 tall, on the rug beside the coffee table.

      How: A tape measure from the floor to the top of its cushion.

    • 09Roughly how many LPs?

      Why we ask

      About 291 in all: 191 in the wall, all face-out (two snug LP crates in bay 3), and 100 in your vinyl stand (50 face-out on top, 50 spine-up between the wires). If there are more, the neatest overflow is another LP column like bay 3's.

      How: A rough count is fine.

    • 10Roughly how many PS2, Xbox 360 and Xbox One games?

      Why we ask

      The game drawer in bay 1 holds about 48 and the two slim drawers in bay 3 about 44 more, face-out: about 92 in all.

      How: A count of each is plenty.

    • 11Wired ports for the projector (master) and the music room (bedroom 2)?

      Projector (master)
      Music room (bedroom 2)

      Why we ask

      Each is one more Cat6 run on the same day as the other two (step 3); easier now than later.

      How: Yes or no for each.

    • 12The 10-gang: is it surge-protected, where are its two switches, and how long is it?

      Surge-protected

      Why we ask

      It now feeds the PC as well as the TV and the modern consoles; if it isn't surge-protected, swap it for one that is. The plan allows 56 cm.

      How: Look for 'surge' on the label; end to end, sockets only.

    • 13Console model numbers, from the labels underneath

      Why we ask

      The rows assume the largest version of each console; real models may free up height.

      How: Photos of the labels are fine.

    • 14The pendant point by the stairs wall: its exact spot

      Out from the stairs wall

      Why we ask

      From your photo it hangs about 55 cm out from the stairs wall, a quarter of the way along the shelf from the stair end. Bar 2 goes on it, over the table if you choose that spot.

      How: Measure from the stairs wall and from the window wall.

    • 15The window corner at floor level: from the pipe boxing to the curtains

      At the floor

      Why we ask

      Thanks for the 25 cm: that's the window ledge, and it's drawn 25 deep (a 22 cm reveal and a 3 cm nose). The one still needed is lower down: your plant stand (98 wide) is drawn with only 4.5 cm a side between the pipe boxing and the curtains when they're open. If it's short, the curtain pole's west end can come in, or swap to layout B.

      How: Tape along the window wall at the floor, from the pipe boxing's face to where the curtains bunch when they're open.

    • 16The RetroTINK-6X CE's size, when it arrives

      Why we ask

      RetroTINK publishes no size; bay 1 allows 23 × 23 × 8 beside the Xbox 360.

      How: Width, depth and height, or a photo with a tape measure.
